subtopics.title: The Concept and Causes of Market Failure

questions.question: Which statement correctly defines market failure?
options: The market produces quantities that differ from the socially optimal quantities
Prices in the market are higher than consumers would like
Some firms in the market make losses
The government intervenes in the market

questions.question: Why does the market fail to supply public goods like streetlights?
options: They are too expensive to build
Non-excludability means no firm can charge users, so the market never forms
The government forbids private streetlights
Consumers do not want them

questions.question: Retrenched mineworkers whose skills fit no other industry illustrate which cause of market failure?
options: Imperfect information
Externalities
Immobility of factors of production
Missing markets

questions.question: Why can a perfectly efficient market still leave essential needs unmet?
options: Because efficient markets always overproduce luxuries
Because efficiency requires shortages
Because prices are always too high in efficient markets
Because markets weigh demand by purchasing power, not by need — efficiency and equity are different tests

subtopics.title: Externalities — Private Against Social Costs and Benefits

questions.question: Social cost equals ...
options: private cost plus external cost
private cost minus external cost
external cost only
private benefit plus external benefit

questions.question: On the negative production externality diagram, where does the marginal social cost curve lie?
options: Below the private cost curve
Parallel above the private cost curve, the gap equal to the external cost per unit
On top of the demand curve
Horizontal at the market price

questions.question: The market outcome for a good with external costs, such as the smoky brick kiln, is ...
options: under-production at too high a price
the socially optimal quantity
over-production at too low a price
zero production

questions.question: Why does the market under-produce education and training?
options: Because students dislike studying
Because colleges are always state-owned
Because training has no private benefit
Because demand counts only the student's private benefit, ignoring the external benefits to employers, communities and the tax base

questions.question: How does a corrective tax equal to the external cost fix over-production?
options: It lifts the private cost curve onto the social cost curve, so the market itself chooses the smaller, correct quantity
It bans the harmful product outright
It transfers the product to state ownership
It lowers the price so consumers buy more

questions.question: No-fee schools and free primary healthcare are examples of which instrument?
options: Maximum prices
Subsidies on goods with external benefits
Corrective taxation
Exchange control

questions.question: A maximum price set below equilibrium typically causes ...
options: surpluses
higher production
shortages and queues
no change in the market

questions.question: The warning that every intervention 'risks replacing a market failure with a government failure' means ...
options: governments should never intervene
markets never actually fail
all interventions succeed if properly announced
each instrument has its own costs and weaknesses, so every intervention must justify itself case by case

questions.question: Why can market prices alone not decide whether a dam or highway should be built?
options: Many of the project's costs and benefits are external, unpriced, or decades in the future
Dams and highways are always unprofitable
Governments are forbidden from using prices
Construction costs are unknowable

questions.question: In CBA, how is time saved by travellers typically valued?
options: It is left out because it has no market price
At the wage the time could have earned
At the price of a bus ticket
At zero, to be conservative

questions.question: Why are future benefits discounted before adding?
options: Because future benefits are imaginary
Because inflation makes future benefits larger
Because a rand received years from now is worth less than a rand today
Because the law requires it

questions.question: Which is a recognised LIMIT of cost-benefit analysis?
options: It counts too many costs and too few benefits
It can only be used for small projects
It requires markets to be perfectly competitive
It totals rands without asking whose rands — a project can pass while its costs fall on the poorest

questions.question: A bag of coal sells for R90 but imposes R7 of coping costs on the neighbouring streets. What is its true social cost?
options: R97 — the R90 private cost plus the R7 external cost
R90, because that is the market price
R83, the price minus the external cost
R7, the external cost alone

questions.question: Because the R7 never appears in the price, the market ...
options: produces the correct amount of coal
sells more coal than the honest price would justify
sells less coal than society wants
stops selling coal entirely

questions.question: The boxing gym's calmer streets and safer evenings, enjoyed by people who never pay membership, are ...
options: private benefits
external costs
external benefits landing on third parties
profits for the gym owner

questions.question: Why does the gym's container stand half-empty at R60 a month?
options: Because nobody in the neighbourhood values fitness
Because the gym is badly run
Because R60 is below the market price
Because members weigh only their private benefit, so the market under-buys a good whose benefits spill over

subtopics.title: Fixing the Price Until It Tells the Truth

questions.question: A R7-per-bag levy on the coal depot, sized to the streets' coping costs, works by ...
options: making the depot's own arithmetic include the dust, so buyers face the honest price and buy less
banning coal sales outright
forcing the depot to relocate
paying the depot to sell more coal

questions.question: Subsidising gym membership from R60 down to R30 is justified because ...
options: gyms deserve government support by right
the neighbourhood keeps a share of the benefit, so society pays for the share it enjoys
cheaper prices are always better
the gym owner requested it

questions.question: "No hauling past the school at drop-off hour, full stop" is an example of ...
options: a corrective tax
a subsidy
regulation — a direct rule for harm too serious to merely tax
direct provision

questions.question: The "smaller failure" sentence reminds us that ...
options: markets always beat governments
governments always beat markets
neither markets nor governments ever fail
both markets and the governments repairing them can fail, so policy chooses the smaller failure case by case

subtopics.title: Should the Toll Road Be Built?

questions.question: Which items belong on the COST side of the toll road's ledger?
options: Construction, the forty expropriated households, the split farm, the bypassed hawkers' lost trade, the noise
Only the tar and the machines
Only the toll fees drivers will pay
Nothing — roads have no social costs

questions.question: Hours not spent in traffic and crashes that never happen are counted as ...
options: costs, because they are hard to measure
benefits, valued in money even though no market prices them
irrelevant to the decision
toll revenue

questions.question: Why does the choice of discount rate deserve its own argument?
options: Because it only affects the construction cost
Because it is set by the toll company
Because turning that one dial can make the same project look golden or worthless
Because it never changes the outcome

questions.question: The highway passes the total test, but the forty moved households carry most of the cost. An honest analyst should ...
options: ignore them, since the total is what matters
cancel the project automatically
recount the benefits until the problem disappears
ask about the losers and about compensating them before the project is approved
